passage: "Sarika, where is your homework notebook?" "Not in my bag." "Why not? You finished it." "If it's not in my bag, Miss can't ask." "Sarika..." "She won't ask. I know." Sangeeta, her mother, held up the notebook. "It's here on the table." Sarika turned her back. "Please leave it." "Miss will ask for it whether it's in your bag or not." Sarika zipped the bag anyway. At pick-up her face was long. "Miss asked. I had no notebook."

qa.q: Where was the homework notebook?
qa.a: The homework notebook was on the table.

qa.q: What did Sarika believe would happen if the notebook was not in her bag?
qa.a: Sarika believed Miss could not ask if the notebook was not in her bag, and she hoped this so much that she would not listen. Her long face at pick-up shows the hope was wrong.

qa.q: What could Sarika do instead, and why?
qa.a: She could put the notebook in the bag and check it off a list. Hoping does not change whether Miss asks, but packing it does.

qa.q: How does the morning look to Sangeeta?
qa.a: Sangeeta sees work that is done and a plan that cannot work, and she cannot talk Sarika out of it. Then she meets a sad child at pick-up. 🙂

grounding: A child leaves the homework notebook out of the bag, hoping Miss will not ask, so hoping takes the place of doing.

passage: On Monday, Zubin came to PE with a dry throat and no water bottle. His friend Pema let him take two sips from hers. That evening Zubin stood in his room with his bag and walked round in a circle. "Now it is maths. Now it is lunch. Now it is PE, and I am running. I am thirsty. I need my bottle!" He fetched the bottle and pushed it in. On Wednesday at PE he took a long drink from his own bottle and gave Pema a thumbs-up.

qa.q: What did Zubin say as he pretended to be at PE?
qa.a: Zubin said, "I am thirsty. I need my bottle!"

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling at PE on Monday?
qa.a: Zubin was thirsty and uncomfortable, since he had no water bottle. Taking two sips from Pema's bottle shows how much he needed it.

qa.q: What other approach could Zubin use to remember his bottle, and why?
qa.a: He could keep a picture list in his bag and tick each item. A list would catch the bottle without needing to imagine the whole day.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Pema?
qa.a: Pema shares two sips out of kindness and later sees Zubin with his own bottle. It may be a relief that the problem was solved.

grounding: After forgetting the water bottle, a child pretends to walk through the school day and sees what is missing.

passage: Asif dragged a chair to the kitchen cupboard, where the jar of sweets sat on the top shelf. He climbed up, stretched, and found he was still too short. He fetched the stool and lifted it onto the chair. His older brother Santosh walked in at that moment. "Stop. Don't climb that, it will tip." Santosh held the chair still and called, "Papa! Asif wants the jar." Papa took the jar down and gave each of them one sweet.

qa.q: What did Asif drag to the cupboard first?
qa.a: Asif dragged a chair to the cupboard first.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when he found he was still too short on the chair?
qa.a: Asif was frustrated but still determined, because he wanted the sweets. He fetched the stool to try again.

qa.q: What safer approach could work, and why?
qa.a: Asif could have called an adult to lift the jar down. A grown-up is tall enough, and a stack of chair and stool could tip.

qa.q: How does the tower look to Santosh?
qa.a: Santosh sees a dangerous stack and a fall waiting to happen. Stopping Asif and calling Papa keeps everyone safe.

grounding: A child tries a chair, then adds a stool, to reach the sweets, and an older brother stops the climb and calls for help.

passage: Devika here, visiting after school. Leela stood in the kitchen under the high shelf and looked up at the jar. Then she turned toward the sitting room. "Papa, can you get the jar down?" She pointed at the shelf. Her father put down his paper, lifted the jar down in one movement and handed her a piece. That was all it took. I do not know whether Leela thought of dragging a chair, or simply knew that asking was easier.

qa.q: What did Leela ask her father?
qa.a: Leela asked, "Papa, can you get the jar down?"

qa.q: What might Leela be feeling as she stands under the shelf and points at the jar?
qa.a: Leela is probably eager for a piece and sure that her father will help. Devika cannot know what else she thought.

qa.q: What could Leela do if nobody was at home, and why?
qa.a: She could wait until a grown-up came home rather than climbing. The jar can be reached safely when someone tall is there.

qa.q: How does the request look to Devika?
qa.a: Devika sees it as quick and simple, with no fuss. Devika cannot tell if Leela thought of another way.

grounding: A child asks Papa to get the jar down and points at the shelf, which is quick and safe.

passage: A power cut had left the house dim, and a torch wobbled over the store-room shelf where a red kite lay just out of reach. Divyansh's older brother Pema took a long bamboo stick, hooked the kite's string and eased it down. Divyansh watched closely. The next evening, his paper plane sat on top of the wardrobe. He fetched the broom, held the handle up, hooked the plane's tail and slid it toward him. "Like Pema!" he said.

qa.q: What did Pema use to bring the kite down?
qa.a: Pema used a long bamboo stick.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling while he watched Pema hook the kite?
qa.a: Divyansh was curious and impressed. He watched closely because he wanted to do the same.

qa.q: What could Divyansh do if the broom handle could not reach, and why?
qa.a: He could ask a grown-up for a longer tool or to lift it down. That is safer than climbing.

qa.q: How does the copying look to Pema?
qa.a: Pema may see a younger brother borrowing the idea and doing well with it. The passage does not say how Pema felt.

grounding: A child sees an older brother use a long stick to hook a kite down and tries a broom handle in the same way.

passage: On Sunday, Avni's father Sachin told her, "If it is too high, ask a grown-up." On Tuesday she stood in the kitchen looking at the biscuit tin on the top shelf. She glanced at the chair by the table. "Too high," she whispered. "Ask a grown-up." She walked to the door and called, "Mummy! Can you get the tin?" On Thursday, at the top shelf of the shoe cupboard, she stopped and called again before she had touched a chair.

qa.q: What did Sachin tell Avni on Sunday?
qa.a: Sachin told her, "If it is too high, ask a grown-up."

qa.q: What was Avni thinking when she glanced at the chair and whispered, "Too high"?
qa.a: She was tempted by the tin but remembered the rule and decided a chair was not the way. Whispering it shows she was working it out for herself.

qa.q: What could Avni do if no grown-up were nearby, and why?
qa.a: She could wait until someone came rather than climb. The rule still says not to try alone.

qa.q: How does Avni's call look to her mother?
qa.a: Avni's mother hears a call for help before anyone climbs, and can come and lift the tin down. It shows the rule is working. 🙂

grounding: A child recalls the earlier rule that if a shelf is too high she asks a grown-up, and calls for mother instead of climbing.

passage: In the village kitchen, Himani stood on tiptoe under a jar on the high shelf. She stretched her arm up and wiggled her fingers. "Grow, arm, grow," she whispered. "If I try hard, my arm will grow long." She stretched until her calves shook. Her brother Sumit, shelling peas by the door, looked up. "That shelf is higher than Papa's head." "They will grow." Himani gave up with a sore shoulder, and the jar had not moved.

qa.q: What did Himani whisper while she stretched?
qa.a: Himani whispered, "Grow, arm, grow."

qa.q: What does Himani want, and what does she think effort will do for her arm?
qa.a: Himani wanted the jar so much that she believed her arm would grow long if she tried hard enough. She did not look at how far the jar was.

qa.q: What could Himani do instead, and why?
qa.a: She could ask Sumit or another grown-up to lift the jar down. The jar is higher than an arm can reach.

qa.q: How does the stretching look to Sumit?
qa.a: Sumit sees a jar much higher than Himani can reach and knows arms do not grow that way. He tries to tell her but she does not listen.

grounding: A child stretches for the jar believing effort will make her arms grow long enough, although the distance is plain.

passage: Kashish stacked a stool on the kitchen chair, climbed up and reached for the jar. The stool shifted under her feet and her stomach lurched. "It's shaking." She gripped the shelf edge and did not move for a second. Then she stepped down very slowly, one foot at a time, and jumped off the chair. She ran to the door. "Usha, come quick! The stool wobbled and I need help." Usha lifted the stool off first, then took the jar down.

qa.q: What happened to the stacked stool?
qa.a: The stool shifted and started to wobble.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when the stool started shaking?
qa.a: Kashish was frightened that she would fall. Her stomach lurched and she gripped the shelf edge.

qa.q: What could Kashish do next time before climbing, and why?
qa.a: She could ask a grown-up first. A stack of furniture can tip, and asking is safer.

qa.q: How does the call look to Usha?
qa.a: Usha hears a call for help before anyone was hurt and can put things right. It may be a relief that Kashish stopped in time.

grounding: A child feels a stacked stool wobble, steps down and calls for help, changing the plan from climbing to asking.

passage: In craft period at school, Omkar folded a sheet of paper in half and pressed the crease flat with the side of his hand. On the front he drew a cake with three candles. Inside he wrote in careful letters, "To Chinmay." Last of all he took the pink and yellow crayons and coloured the cake and the flames. The teacher walked past. "Lovely." Omkar held the card up at arm's length and looked at it.

qa.q: What did Omkar draw on the front of the card?
qa.a: Omkar drew a cake with three candles.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling as he held the card up at arm's length?
qa.a: Omkar felt proud and pleased with his card. He looked at it carefully after finishing.

qa.q: What could Omkar do if he was not sure what to write inside, and why?
qa.a: He could ask the teacher for ideas or look at another child's card. A word or two can help a card feel finished.

qa.q: How would the card look to Chinmay?
qa.a: Chinmay would get a card with a name inside and a cake with candles. It shows that someone remembered.

grounding: A child folds the paper, draws a cake, writes Chinmay's name inside and colours last so the card comes together.

passage: Reena bent over her paper. "What are you drawing?" asked her sister Kashish. "Dadi's card," said Reena. "I'm pretending she opens it. She goes, ooh!" "What's she looking at?" "Flowers. Dadi loves marigolds, the orange and yellow ones. So I'll use orange and yellow." She drew a big marigold and grinned. "And DADI on top in big letters, so she can read it without her glasses." Kashish laughed. "She'll keep it on her shelf." "That's what I'm making it for."

qa.q: Which flowers did Reena choose for the card?
qa.a: Reena chose marigolds, the orange and yellow ones.

qa.q: What does Reena imagine Dadi feeling as she opens the card?
qa.a: Reena imagines Dadi smiling and delighted, saying, "ooh!" She picks the drawing to match.

qa.q: What other approach could help Reena choose a design, and why?
qa.a: Reena could ask Kashish or a grown-up what Dadi likes. Someone who knows Dadi can add ideas.

qa.q: How does Reena's plan look to Kashish?
qa.a: Kashish is amused by how carefully Reena thinks of Dadi, right down to the glasses. Kashish sees a card that will be kept.

grounding: A child imagines Dadi opening the card and smiling, and picks her favourite flowers and colours for the drawing.
